checkpoints: Plain Kubernetes Deployment only has two strategies: RollingUpdate (replaces pods by maxSurge/maxUnavailable, with no precise control over the traffic percentage at any given moment) or Recreate (tear down everything, then recreate).
Deployment has no concept of "pause to observe" or "auto-analyze before proceeding" — once a rollout starts, it runs to completion with no deliberate stopping point.

Rollout is a dedicated Custom Resource Definition (CRD) from Argo Rollouts — because native Kubernetes knows nothing about steps/setWeight/pause/analysis, a separate controller (the argo-rollouts controller) must run in the cluster to read the Rollout object and execute that exact logic, something kube-controller-manager doesn't do by default.

While a canary step is in progress (e.g. currently at setWeight: 20), at the ReplicaSet level TWO ReplicaSets coexist in parallel with clearly different roles: one stable ReplicaSet (the previously-running version, holding roughly 80% of traffic) and one canary ReplicaSet (the new version, holding exactly 20% of traffic per the current weight) — unlike a regular rolling update, where it's just "the old ReplicaSet shrinking, the new one growing", with no concept of a deliberately fixed traffic percentage.
In exchange for installing the extra controller, you get proactive pause steps (pause) for human observation before proceeding.
You also get an automatic analysis gate (analysis) based on real SLIs (Prometheus) to auto-decide promote vs. rollback — two things a plain Deployment is entirely incapable of.
It's true `helm install` still works with hard-coded values — Helm just renders the Go template into a YAML manifest and `kubectl apply`s it, so it doesn't force you to use `values.yaml`.

But it isn't a proper chart: the problem surfaces the moment you need the chart for a second environment, since the only way to change replicas/image there is to edit `templates/deployment.yaml` directly.

That means the chart is no longer "one shared copy" — each environment ends up with its own hand-edited version, or someone must remember to edit it before every install, which is error-prone and a source of drift between environments.
The fix: move every value that differs between environments into `values.yaml` as defaults (e.g. `replicas: 3`, `image: { repository: myapp, tag: 1.2.0 }`).
The template should only reference those values via `{{ .Values.replicas }}` and `{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}`, with no hard-coded numbers or strings left in it.

Each environment then just needs its own values file (e.g. `values-staging.yaml` with `replicas: 1`, `values-prod.yaml` with `replicas: 5`) to override the defaults via `helm install -f values-staging.yaml`, without touching the original template.

Core principle: the template is the fixed, reusable part while only `values` changes per environment — correctly separating the two is the required condition for one chart to run across multiple environments without forking code or hand-editing before every deploy.
Final answer: the winning image tag is 2.0.1.
Precedence rule among -f/--values files: a file listed LATER on the command line overrides one listed earlier.
Applying that rule to the two files: between values.yaml (1.0.0) and values-prod.yaml (1.5.0), values-prod.yaml would win on a file-only basis, since it's listed later.
--set (and its variants --set-string, --set-file) always has the HIGHEST precedence, overriding the contents of ALL -f/--values files.

That --set precedence is absolute/fixed, not positional — it wins regardless of where --set is written relative to the -f flags on the command line, unlike the -f-vs-f ordering rule which does depend on position.
Because of that absolute precedence, --set image.tag=2.0.1 overrides both values-prod.yaml's 1.5.0 and values.yaml's 1.0.0.

Practical lesson: --set is convenient for quick/temporary overrides but risks unexpected surprises when it's buried in a CI/CD command, so prefer explicit values files for pipelines and reserve --set for temporary, clearly-logged overrides.

Helm uses a TEMPLATING model: chart templates (`templates/*.yaml`) are written in Go template syntax (`{{ .Values.x }}`, `{{ range }}`, `{{ include }}`) parameterized via `values.yaml`, and the template file is NOT valid Kubernetes YAML until rendered.

Helm's core strength is PACKAGING and DISTRIBUTION: a chart can be versioned, published to a Helm repo, and installed by many different consumers with entirely different parameter sets (via `--set`/`-f`) without needing to know its internals.
Kustomize is TEMPLATE-FREE: the base is plain Kubernetes YAML that is directly readable with no rendering step at all.

Kustomize overlays (dev/stg/prod) declare only the differences as patches (strategic merge patch or JSON6902), assembled via `kustomization.yaml` — and unlike Helm, both base and overlay stay valid Kubernetes YAML that can be `git diff`'d intuitively, with no template language to learn or guess the rendering of.

For use case (1) (packaging an app for many teams to self-install with their own parameters), pick Helm, since this is exactly the 'one chart, many consumers, many parameter sets' problem plus chart versioning/publishing that Kustomize has no equivalent for.

For use case (2) (managing 3 environments dev/stg/prod for one team's own app differing by a few small fields), pick Kustomize, since there is no need for templating machinery — a base plus 3 short overlays is easy to review on Git.
General selection principle: distributing to many parties with diverse parameters calls for Helm, while managing a few internal variants of the same app calls for Kustomize.

Parse the error mechanically: `doc is missing path: /spec/template/spec/containers/1/image` means the JSON6902 `replace` op targets array index `1`, but path resolution fails because no element exists at that index in the rendered document.

Cross-reference `base/deployment.yaml` to find why: the `web` Deployment defines only ONE container, so the `containers` array only has index `0` — index `1` was never there, which is the root of the error.

Explain the underlying addressing model: JSON6902 identifies edit locations by absolute path + numeric array index, not by matching an identifying field (e.g. `name`) the way a strategic merge patch would.

State the consequence of that model: the path must exactly mirror the document's current structure (element count and order), so one wrong index fails the patch immediately with no fuzzy-match fallback.
Give the fix: change `path` to `/spec/template/spec/containers/0/image`, the correct index for the single existing `web` container.
Specify the verification step: rerun `kubectl kustomize overlays/prod` and confirm it renders cleanly with `image: myapp:2.0.0-prod` on the `web` container.

Flag the long-term fragility: if the base later adds a second container (e.g. a sidecar), index-`0` patching can silently hit the wrong container if declaration order changes — prefer a strategic merge patch matching explicitly by `name: web` for fields prone to structural change.
The core bug: the `mychart.name` helper returns a FIXED STRING `myapp`, never referencing `.Release.Name` or `.Values.nameOverride`.
Direct consequence: every release of this chart, no matter what release name is used at `helm install <release-name>`, produces an identical Deployment with `metadata.name: myapp`.

Collision setup: if team A and team B each install the chart under different release names (e.g. `team-a-release`, `team-b-release`) in the SAME namespace, both try to create a Deployment named `myapp`.

Two possible failure outcomes from that collision: the later release errors that the resource already exists (owned by the other release) — or, worse, if Helm can't detect the ownership mismatch, it silently "takes over" and modifies the other release's resource.

The label `app: myapp` is also hard-coded identically, so the Deployment's `selector.matchLabels` (and any Service sharing this pattern) risk matching the WRONG pods belonging to a different release with the same label, causing traffic to be misrouted between two supposedly independent releases.

The standard Helm fix (matching the default `helm create` template) is to add a `mychart.fullname` helper that combines `.Release.Name` with the chart name — logic equivalent to `{{- if .Values.fullnameOverride -}}{{ .Values.fullnameOverride }}{{- else -}}{{ .Release.Name }}-{{ .Chart.Name }}{{- end -}}` (shortened if they match).

Applying the fix means replacing EVERY `mychart.name` reference with `mychart.fullname` in `metadata.name` and in the `app.kubernetes.io/instance`/`app.kubernetes.io/name` labels, so each release ends up with a UNIQUE resource name and label tied to its own `Release.Name`.

To verify, install two differently-named releases (`rel-a`, `rel-b`) in the same namespace on a test cluster and confirm `kubectl get deploy` shows two distinctly-named Deployments with no collision or cross-routing.

Diagnose the root cause: without `--atomic`/`--wait`, Helm considers the upgrade "successful" as soon as the API server ACCEPTS the new manifest (returns 200 OK), without waiting to see if the new pods actually become Ready.

Explain the consequence: with a broken image, the new ReplicaSet gets stuck in CrashLoopBackOff and the Deployment stalls half-old/half-new, while the pipeline has already reported "deploy successful" — leaving the incident to be caught and fixed only by someone manually running `helm rollback`.
Main fix: add the `--atomic` flag, which forces Helm to wait until every resource (Deployment, pods) actually reaches Ready state before considering the upgrade successful.
`--atomic` also makes Helm automatically roll back to the immediately prior revision if the rollout still isn't Ready after the wait period — no on-call human needed.

Because `--atomic` waits until `--timeout` expires before declaring failure, set an explicit `--timeout` (e.g. 5m) instead of relying on Helm's default, sized to the app's actually-measured startup time (readinessProbe + warm-up time): too short wrongly rolls back a rollout that's just slow-but-fine, too long delays how quickly production self-heals.

Verification plan: deploy a deliberately-broken `IMAGE_TAG` on staging with the new command and confirm Helm auto-rolls-back to the correct old revision (cross-checked via `helm history myapp` showing the new revision marked then reverted), with zero manual steps.
`resources: [../../base]` loads the entire original base manifest as the foundation for the overlay.
Requirement (1) replica count uses the `patches` field — a JSON6902 `replace` at `/spec/replicas` targeting the `web` Deployment (or equivalently a strategic-merge patch with `spec.replicas: 5`).
Requirement (2) image tag uses the dedicated `images` field (`name: myapp`, `newTag: "2.0.0"`) instead of a hand-written patch.
The `images.name` value must match the image name referenced in the base manifest (`myapp`), NOT the container's name — a distinct point many answers conflate.
Kustomize's `images` field automatically finds and rewrites every reference to that image across all resources, which is precisely how requirement (2) is satisfied without writing a dedicated patch.

Requirement (3) name prefix uses `namePrefix: prod-`, which auto-prepends `prod-` to `metadata.name` of every resource AND auto-updates cross-resource references between renamed resources (e.g. a Deployment's `configMapRef` still correctly points at the renamed ConfigMap), instead of editing each resource by hand.
Requirement (4) ConfigMap override uses `configMapGenerator` with `behavior: merge` and `literals: [LOG_LEVEL=warn]`, merging into the existing `app-config` rather than overwriting it wholesale.

The generated ConfigMap gets a content-based hash suffix that Kustomize auto-propagates into every Deployment referencing it, so a content change produces a new name and forces a rolling restart to pick up the new config.
Before rolling back, run `helm history <release-name>` first to see the full revision list (revision number, timestamp, description, status) instead of rolling back blindly.
From that history output, precisely identify which revision number is the current broken one and which is the correct prior good one, based on the actual numbers shown rather than guessing.
Run `helm rollback <release-name> <revision-number>` with the specific revision number identified, rather than issuing the command with no number.

Know that omitting the revision number is still valid and defaults to the immediately prior revision, but being explicit is safer — it avoids confusion when multiple people might be operating on the same release.

Understand that rollback does not delete history or literally rewind time — it creates a new revision with content identical to the selected old revision and applies it like a regular upgrade, so `helm history` afterward shows a new line added rather than old revisions being erased.
Confirm success by checking `helm history` shows the newest revision with status `deployed` and the expected description.
Cross-check with `kubectl get pods` to see the new pods Running/Ready.

Most importantly, verify the application in practice (call the API, check logs, or however the team verifies the bug) to be sure it's actually fixed, rather than just trusting Kubernetes' reported state.
RTO and RPO measure two completely different axes even though both are expressed in time units

RTO (Recovery Time Objective) measures the DOWNTIME axis: how long the system is allowed to be down, i.e. the time from when the incident happens to when the system is fully recovered and serving again
RPO (Recovery Point Objective) measures the DATA-LOSS axis: how much data is allowed to be lost, i.e. the gap between the most recent backup and the moment the incident happens

Concrete example setup: with backups every 24h (at midnight) and an incident at 11pm the same day, RPO is nearly 24 hours — every data change since the last backup up to the incident is permanently lost when restoring from that backup

In that same example, restore duration (whether the restore itself takes 10 minutes or 3 hours) does not change how much data was lost — restore speed is purely an RTO matter, entirely unrelated to RPO

Because RTO and RPO are independent axes, a system can have a short RTO but a long RPO (fast restore process but infrequent/sparse backups), or the reverse — a short RPO but a long RTO (near-continuous backups but a manual, untested, slow restore process)

Improving RPO requires increasing backup frequency (or near-real-time replication), while improving RTO requires optimizing the restore process (automation, restore drills) — these are two different efforts, and improving one does not automatically improve the other
